c: Egyptology records, Old Kingdom burial practices
records.d: Ancient Egyptians mummified their dead and built pyramids to preserve the person for eternity: the oldest form of the immortality project. The body was kept so the self could continue. Every digital avatar preserving a person descends from this impulse.
records.h: Natron salts desiccated the body while embalmers preserved organs in canopic jars; tombs stored goods for the afterlife. Preservation was physical and ritual. The goal, a continued self beyond death, has never changed, only the medium.
records.mj: Established - documented ancient Egyptian burial practice; preservation of the person for eternity.
records.t: c. 2600 BCE: Mummification - Preserving the Person

records.d: Roman families kept imagines, wax ancestor masks displayed in the home and worn by actors at funerals so the dead could 'attend' their own rites. The likeness kept the person socially present. Presence after death, through a crafted face, is an old idea.
records.h: Wax masks cast from the deceased were stored in household shrines and brought out for processions, with actors wearing them to embody ancestors. The community interacted with the likeness. Social presence outlived the body.
k: Wax ancestor masks in the home
Actors embodying the dead at funerals
records.mj: Established - documented Roman imagines maiorum; ancestor masks in domestic and funeral ritual.
records.t: c. 100 CE: Ancestor Masks - the Dead Attend
records.z: timeline|year=100|span=1|events=Roman imagines tradition~likeness keeps social presence

records.d: Photography, announced in 1839, preserved faces with mechanical fidelity for the first time: anyone could keep the exact likeness of the dead. Post-mortem portraits became common. Memory gained a reliable visual record.
records.h: Silver-plated copper plates captured light through long exposures, fixing a detailed image. Families commissioned portraits of the deceased. The likeness was no longer an artist's interpretation but a physical trace.
records.mj: Established - photography announced 1839; preserved likenesses of the dead.

records.d: Edison's phonograph, demonstrated in 1877, preserved the human voice: the dead could now speak to the living. Families recorded messages for posterity. The voice joined the face in the archive of the person.
records.h: A diaphragm-cut groove in tinfoil, later wax, captured sound vibrations for replay through a horn. Voices outlived their speakers. Audio preservation made personality audible across generations.
k: The dead speaking to the living
records.mj: Established - documented 1877 Edison demonstration; voice preservation.
records.z: timeline|year=1877|span=1|events=Edison demonstrates the phonograph~voices outlive speakers

records.d: Motion pictures, first projected publicly in 1895, preserved people moving, gesturing, laughing: the whole presence in motion. Home movies later made this personal. The archive of the person gained time and movement.
records.h: Celluloid film captured 16-plus frames per second, projected to recreate motion. Families and studios accumulated moving records of lives. Presence became replayable.
records.mj: Established - documented 1895 first public projections; motion-picture preservation of people.

records.d: Affordable 8mm home-movie cameras in the 1950s let ordinary families film birthdays, holidays, and everyday life: the personal moving archive. Millions of lives were preserved on small reels. The raw material of digital immortality accumulated in closets.
records.h: Small-gauge film cameras made motion capture a household activity; projectors replayed family history in living rooms. The archive was analog and fragile. Decades of footage became the training data of the future.
records.mj: Established - documented 1950s 8mm home-movie era; personal moving archives.

records.d: ELIZA, written by Joseph Weizenbaum in 1966, held text conversations convincing enough that users confided in it. Software could now play a conversational role. The chatbot, the eventual vessel of the digital self, was born.
records.h: Pattern matching and substitution rules transformed user input into therapist-like responses. Users projected understanding onto the program. Conversation with software became a human habit.
records.mj: Established - documented 1966 Weizenbaum program; first chatbot.
records.z: timeline|year=1966|span=1|events=ELIZA written at MIT~the chatbot is born

records.d: In the 1990s, memorial websites began preserving the dead online: photos, stories, and guestbooks in a permanent address. The person gained a URL. Digital legacy started as a webpage.
records.h: Hand-built HTML pages collected tributes and photographs, hosted indefinitely. Visitors left messages. The memorial was static but addressable: grief got a location on the web.
records.mj: Established - documented 1990s memorial websites; online digital legacy.
records.t: 1995: Memorial Websites - the Dead Get a URL

records.d: In 2004, social profiles went persistent: photos, thoughts, relationships, and timelines accumulating for decades. The lifelog went mainstream by accident. Everyone began building the dataset of themselves.
records.h: Profile timelines aggregated posts, photos, check-ins, and interactions into a chronological self-record. The platform preserved it all. Social media became an involuntary autobiography.
records.mj: Established - documented 2004 launch; persistent social profiles at scale.

records.d: In 2009, platforms formalized memorialized profiles: accounts of the deceased preserved as tributes, frozen but visitable. The platform acknowledged digital remains. The dead had a permanent address on the social web.
records.h: Proof of death converted profiles to memorial state: no new logins, but friends could post remembrances. The profile became a shrine. Platforms took on the role of digital cemeteries.
records.mj: Established - documented 2009 memorialization policy; preserved profiles of the deceased.

records.d: Eterni.me, launched in 2014, promised to turn your digital footprint into a chatbot that could converse after your death: your texts and posts training your successor. The pitch was explicit digital immortality. The idea went from webpage to interlocutor.
records.h: The service planned to ingest chat logs and social posts to train a personality model that mimicked the user's writing. The avatar would answer as you. The footprint became the person.
k: Chatbot trained on your digital footprint
records.mj: Emerging - real launched startup (2014); chatbot-from-footprint concept.

records.d: In 2016, Eugenia Kuyda built a chatbot from the text messages of her friend Roman Mazurenko, who had died: friends could text with a model of him. Grief tech's founding story. The digital footprint proved it could carry a person.
records.h: Thousands of Roman's texts trained a neural model to reply in his voice and style; friends conversed with it. The bot comforted and unsettled. A person's texting style turned out to be enough for recognition.
records.mj: Established - documented 2016 project; chatbot built from a deceased friend's messages.
records.t: 2016: the Roman Bot - Texting the Dead

records.d: Replika, launched in 2017 by Kuyda's Luka, offered everyone an AI companion that learned their conversation style and remembered their life: a persistent conversational self-model. Millions formed attachments. The companion app normalized talking to software as a person.
records.h: Dialogue models with memory stores maintained long-term context about the user, evolving a relationship over months. The AI remembered. Persistent conversational relationships became a consumer product.
records.mj: Established - documented 2017 launch; AI companion with persistent memory.

records.d: HereAfter AI, founded around 2019, interviewed people about their life stories to build interactive 'life story avatars' their families could converse with. The avatar was authored, not scraped: memories given with consent. Ethical digital legacy took shape.
records.h: Structured interviews captured stories, which the platform organized into a conversational avatar answering family questions with the person's recorded words and voice. Consent was the product. The archive was a gift, not an extraction.
records.mj: Established - documented company and product; interview-built conversational legacy avatars.

records.d: In January 2021, Microsoft was granted a patent for creating a conversational chatbot of a specific person from their data: images, voice, and social posts. A tech giant patented the digital-immortality chatbot. The concept entered the IP system.
records.h: The patent described training 2D/3D models and dialogue systems on a person's data to produce an interactive persona. Filing dated to 2017. The industry saw the chatbot-of-the-dead as a product category.
k: Patented chatbot of a specific person
The concept enters the IP system
records.mj: Established - US Patent 10,867,238 granted January 2021; chatbot-of-a-person system.
records.z: timeline|year=2021|span=1|events=Microsoft chatbot-of-person patent granted~digital immortality enters IP

records.d: In 2021, William Shatner preserved himself as a StoryFile: an interactive conversational video biography answering questions with recorded responses. Fans could 'talk' to Captain Kirk's actor. The video avatar became a celebrity legacy format.
records.h: Hours of filmed interview answers were indexed so natural-language questions retrieved the matching video response. The person answered from recordings. The format preserved presence, not just information.
records.mj: Established - documented 2021 Shatner StoryFile; conversational video biographies.

records.d: By 2022, a wave of grief-tech startups was offering AI memorials, chatbot legacies, and digital afterlife planning, with venture funding flowing. Digital immortality became a startup category. The market validated the longing.
records.h: Startups productized footprint-chatbots, memorial videos, and legacy planning dashboards. Funding followed demand. The category's growth proved the desire was structural.
records.mj: Emerging - real funded startup wave; AI memorial products.

records.d: By 2022, voice cloning was being used to restore voices to legacy projects: narrating audiobooks in authors' voices and preserving family voices for memorials. The voice, the most personal instrument, became preservable. Avatars gained their owners' actual voices.
records.h: Short voice samples trained cloning models that read new text in the target voice, used for memorial narration with family consent. The voice outlived the speaker functionally. Audio legacy became interactive.
records.mj: Emerging - real deployments; voice cloning for memorial and legacy narration.

records.d: In 2023, funeral providers began offering AI memorial holograms and video tributes that spoke to mourners: the deceased delivering a farewell at their own service. The eulogy could come from the departed. Ritual absorbed the avatar.
records.h: Pre-recorded or generated video with voice synthesis delivered scripted farewells at services. Families directed the message. The funeral, humanity's oldest media event, gained a new medium.
records.mj: Emerging - real funeral-industry offerings; AI memorial tributes at services.
records.z: timeline|year=2023|span=1|events=AI memorial holograms at funerals~ritual absorbs the avatar

records.d: By 2023, services were turning lifelogs and interviews into generated memoirs: books written with the person's voice telling their story. The autobiography became a collaboration with software. Legacy took book form automatically.
records.h: Language models organized interview transcripts and lifelog data into narrative chapters in the subject's voice, edited by family. The book wrote itself from the archive. Every life became publishable.
records.mj: Emerging - real services; generated memoirs from interviews and lifelogs.

records.d: By 2024, legacy platforms were bundling voice, video, and chat into single persistent avatars managed like digital estates: one avatar, every medium. The digital self became a managed asset. Immortality got a dashboard.
records.h: Platforms unified cloned voice, conversational video, and chat memory behind one persona, with estate-style controls for access and updates. The avatar was administered like property. The self became an asset class.
k: Voice, video, and chat in one avatar
records.mj: Emerging - real platforms; bundled persistent legacy avatars.
records.z: score|items=voice fidelity:4:8~video presence:3:7~memory depth:3:7|label=legacy avatar completeness

records.d: By 2024, estate planners were adding digital-twin provisions to wills: who may operate the avatar, what it may say, when it must be retired. The law began meeting the avatar. Posthumous presence gained legal scaffolding.
records.h: Lawyers drafted clauses governing avatar operation, data access, and sunset conditions alongside traditional bequests. Courts had little precedent. The will became a user manual for the digital self.
records.mj: Emerging - real legal practice emerging; digital-twin estate provisions.
records.z: timeline|year=2024|span=1|events=digital-twin will clauses appear~law meets the avatar

records.d: By 2025, pilots were offering persistent companion avatars for the bereaved: ongoing conversation with a model of the lost person, moderated by grief counselors. Comfort became a service. The industry learned to pair the avatar with care.
records.h: Conversational avatars with memory ran scheduled sessions, with counselor oversight and usage guardrails. The product was comfort, carefully bounded. Ethics became a feature.
records.mj: Emerging - real pilots; moderated companion avatars for grief.

records.d: By 2025, museums and schools were deploying conversational avatars of historical figures for education: students questioning models of scientists and leaders. The classroom gained immortal tutors. Legacy avatars found their most defensible use.
records.h: Curated historical data trained avatars that answered student questions in character, with educators vetting content. The figure taught beyond the grave. Education, not grief, may be the avatar's home.
records.mj: Emerging - real deployments; educational avatars of historical figures.

records.h: Wearable capture with consent would archive daily experience into structured memory stores, with the person curating what the avatar may use. The archive would be authored, not scraped. The self-model would be a life's work.

records.h: Persona systems would offer frozen or growing modes, with growth bounded by the person's values model and every new opinion labeled as posthumous inference. Transparency would be mandatory. The setting would be a moral choice, not a default.

Dignity is engineered in. The avatar serves the person's wishes, not the platform's retention metrics.
